title: Demonstrate the ability to start and run a business and adapt to a changing business environment

lessons.title: Starting your business
lessons.html:
Starting your business

Once you have chosen a good idea, you need to get ready to start. A simple plan helps you think before you spend money.

Make a simple business plan

  1. What will I sell? For example, fresh vegetables: spinach, cabbage and tomatoes.
  2. Who will buy? Farm workers, the spaza shop, the school kitchen.
  3. What do I need? Seed, a fenced plot, water, a spade, a hosepipe.
  4. How much will it cost? Write down every cost.
  5. Where will the money come from? Savings, a stokvel, or a small loan you can pay back.
  6. What price will I charge? The price must cover costs and leave a profit.

Register and follow the rules

Small businesses may need to follow local rules, for example a trading permit from the municipality for selling at a market. Ask at the municipal office or a local business support centre. Never sell food that is spoiled or dirty.

Keep money separate

Keep the business money apart from your household money. Use a separate tin, envelope or bank account. If you mix them, you will not know if the business is making a profit.

Keep records

Every day, write down:

  • what you bought and how much it cost;
  • what you sold and how much you got;
  • who owes you money.

At the end of the month add up money in and money out. Money in minus money out is your profit (or loss).

Example

Bheki spent R600 on seed, fertiliser and a hosepipe. In the first month he sold vegetables for R1 100. His profit was R500. He put R200 back into the business to buy more seed.

lessons.title: Running the business and adapting to change
lessons.html:
Running the business and adapting to change

Running a business means doing the same important jobs well every day: buying, producing, selling, keeping records and looking after customers.

Look after your customers

  • Sell good quality every time.
  • Be there when you said you would be, for example every pay day.
  • Be friendly and give the right change.
  • Be careful with credit. If you give credit, write it down and agree when they will pay.

Things change

The business environment is everything around your business that you do not control. It changes all the time:

  • Weather: drought or hail can destroy crops.
  • Prices: fertiliser, feed and fuel prices can go up.
  • Competition: someone else may start selling the same thing.
  • Customers: people may want different products, or have less money in January.
  • Rules: new rules may come from the municipality or government.

How to adapt

  1. Watch your records. If sales drop, find out why.
  2. Talk to customers and ask what they want.
  3. Change your product or price if needed, for example sell smaller bunches that cost less.
  4. Find cheaper inputs, or buy together with other small farmers.
  5. Do not depend on one product only. Bheki added green mealies in summer so he still had something to sell when cabbage prices dropped.
  6. Save some profit for bad times.

Adapting does not mean giving up. It means changing the way you work so the business can keep going.

Key points

  • Make a simple plan before you start: product, customers, needs, costs, money, price.
  • Keep business money separate and write down every sale and cost.
  • Profit is money in minus money out.
  • The business environment changes: weather, prices, competition, customers and rules.
  • Adapt by watching records, listening to customers and changing what you do.
